reading.title: Posters for the Book Swap
reading.purpose: See how a library club chooses honest persuasion over flashy tricks.
paras: The seventh-grade library club had one week to advertise its spring book swap. Spread across the worktable were markers, poster board, and three rough drafts. Jordan held up his sketch first. Across the top, bold red letters shouted a sensational headline designed to shock passersby: "READ THIS OR MISS THE BIGGEST EVENT IN SCHOOL HISTORY!" Beneath it sat a short slogan: "Trade Old Pages, Win New Worlds."

Elena shook her head and tapped the red letters. "The slogan is catchy, Jordan, but the headline feels deceptive," she said. "It gives a false impression that we are handing out giant prizes. If students show up expecting a carnival, they will leave annoyed." She pointed out that even the word "old" carried a dusty connotation, suggesting worn-out junk instead of favorite stories worth sharing.

"Okay, then how do we sway people to bring books?" Jordan asked. "We need something compelling enough to make classmates stop in the hallway." Elena suggested an honest incentive, a small reward that encourages action: every student who donated two books would receive a handmade bookmark and early entry on Friday morning. She also asked the soccer captain to endorse the event over morning announcements, since younger grades trusted his advice.

Their advisor, Ms. Lin, stopped by and praised the shift. "One-sided propaganda hides the truth just to push a crowd," she told them. "Good persuasion respects the audience." Elena asked two sixth graders who loved last year's swap to write a short testimonial, a real quote praising how many mysteries they found. By Thursday afternoon, the club hung calm, clear posters that promised exactly what the library could deliver—and by Friday morning, the donation bins were already overflowing.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "incentive" most nearly means
choices: a loud headline written in giant red letters
a small reward offered to encourage action
a warning that an event is about to close
a short poem printed on the back of a book
qs.why: Paragraph 3 defines incentive directly as "a small reward that encourages action."

qs.q: Which sentence shows why Elena objected to using the word "old" on the poster?
choices: Elena shook her head and tapped the red letters.
It gives a false impression that we are handing out giant prizes.
If students show up expecting a carnival, they will leave annoyed.
She pointed out that even the word "old" carried a dusty connotation, suggesting worn-out junk instead of favorite stories worth sharing.
qs.why: This sentence explains the unwanted feeling the word "old" suggests to readers.

ev.text: She pointed out that even the word "old" carried a dusty connotation, suggesting worn-out junk instead of favorite stories worth sharing.

qs.q: What does the overflowing donation bin on Friday morning suggest?
choices: Honest, clear persuasion worked well without needing exaggerated headlines.
Students only donated books because they hoped to win a giant carnival prize.
The soccer captain brought most of the mystery novels from his own house.
Classmates ignored the posters and came only after Ms. Lin announced the swap.
qs.why: The club replaced the sensational headline with clear promises, real quotes, and a modest reward, and the swap still succeeded.

qs.q: What is the main theme of this story?
choices: Catchy slogans are useless unless they are printed in bright red letters.
Sports captains should always be in charge of school library fundraisers.
Respectful, truthful persuasion builds trust better than exaggeration does.
Book swaps only succeed when sixth graders write all of the hallway posters.
qs.why: The club moves away from sensational, deceptive claims toward honest incentives and real testimonials, earning strong turnout.

clues.text: a small reward that encourages action
a real quote praising how many mysteries they found
